finding.claim: PUT /me copies every key of req.body onto req.user with Object.assign and persists it, so any authenticated user can overwrite privilege or ownership fields (role, isAdmin, orgId, email, id) if the user model has them.
finding.source: req.body on PUT /me (JSON body from the authenticated caller)
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) at users.js:5, persisted by req.store.save(req.user) at users.js:6

trace.note: PUT /me handler receives req.body; no auth check visible in this file
Object.assign copies all own enumerable body keys onto req.user
req.store.save persists the modified user record
res.json returns the full modified record

finding.guards_checked: No field allowlist, schema validation, role check per field, or protected-field list in users.js. The sibling /me/profile route (users.js:12) uses an explicit allowlist, so the safe pattern exists but is not applied here. Auth middleware, body parser, and user model are not in the repo and could not be checked; the finding assumes req.user is the authenticated user and that privilege fields exist.

verdict.guard_found: None in users.js. PUT /me (users.js:4-8) has no field allowlist, schema check, or per-field role check. The allowlist at users.js:11-12 belongs to /me/profile, not /me. Auth middleware and the user model are not in the repo.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches users.js:4-7: Object.assign at line 5 copies the whole req.body onto req.user, and line 6 saves it, with no guard in this file. Whether the attacker gains anything depends on the user model having privilege or ownership fields (role, isAdmin, orgId) and on the auth middleware setting req.user, and neither is in the repo, so the finding cannot be confirmed or refuted from the code available.

finding.claim: A __proto__ own key in the PUT /me JSON body makes Object.assign invoke the __proto__ setter on req.user, replacing its prototype with attacker-controlled data for the rest of the request.
finding.source: JSON body key "__proto__" on PUT /me, parsed as an own property by express.json

trace.note: Object.assign sets req.user.__proto__ via the setter, changing its prototype
Persistence does not serialize the prototype, so impact is limited to in-memory reads in later code
Response reads req.user; inherited attacker properties could appear

finding.guards_checked: No __proto__, constructor, or prototype key filtering in this file. Global Object.prototype is not polluted by this path. Impact depends on downstream checks that read unset properties (for example req.user.isAdmin), which are not in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: none. There is no __proto__ filtering in users.js, but the impact is nil. Line 5 does invoke the Object.prototype.__proto__ setter, so the mechanism itself is real. Line 7 (`res.json(req.user)`) serializes only own enumerable properties, so inherited attacker properties never reach the response.
verdict.reason: The mechanism at users.js:5 is real (Object.assign uses [[Set]], so the __proto__ setter fires and changes req.user's prototype), but the trace is wrong at users.js:7 because res.json/JSON.stringify emits only own properties, and the only later use in the handler is that serialization, so nothing in the repo reads the swapped prototype. The attacker is also the account owner modifying their own req.user object, with no cross-user or privilege effect shown, so there is no reachable vulnerability as claimed.

finding.claim: PUT /me/profile with omitted displayName or bio sets those fields to undefined, clearing the user's existing profile data.
finding.source: Omitted or empty displayName/bio keys in the PUT /me/profile body
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, { displayName, bio }) at users.js:12, persisted at users.js:13

trace.note: Destructures displayName and bio, which are undefined when absent
Object.assign copies undefined values, overwriting existing data

finding.guards_checked: No check that a field was provided before overwriting. Affects only the caller's own record, so this is an integrity issue, not cross-user.

verdict.guard_found: none: users.js:10-15 has no check on which fields are present, and no other file exists in the directory to supply one. Still, the attacker is the authenticated user writing their own record (users.js:13 saves req.user), so this is not a security vulnerability.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: Object.assign at users.js:12 copies undefined values from the destructured fields at users.js:11, and users.js:13 persists them. But the only party affected is the caller clearing their own profile (users.js:13 saves req.user), a role that already has that power, so this is a partial-update correctness bug rather than a vulnerability, and it should not be reported as a security finding.

finding.claim: displayName and bio are stored without type or length validation, so objects, arrays, or very large strings can be persisted and may be unsafe where the store or renderer trusts these fields.
finding.source: displayName and bio in the PUT /me/profile JSON body
finding.sink: Stored via Object.assign and req.store.save at users.js:12-13

trace.note: Fields taken from req.body without type checks

finding.guards_checked: No type, length, or format validation in this file. Store and rendering behavior are not in the repo, so exploitability is unconfirmed.

verdict.guard_found: none. No type, length, or format check exists in users.js:10-15, and the only file in the directory is users.js, so the auth middleware (which sets req.user and req.store) and the store/renderer are not present.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: users.js:11 destructures displayName and bio from req.body unchecked, users.js:12 assigns them to req.user, and users.js:13 persists them via req.store.save. No validation exists in the repo, but the claimed harm depends on store or renderer behavior that is not in the code available (only users.js:1-17 is present), and the attacker is presumably an authenticated user only able to write their own profile, so the impact is unproven.

finding.claim: Responses serialize the entire req.user object, which may include secret fields such as password hashes or reset tokens if the stored record contains them.
finding.source: Not attacker-controlled; the exposure is of stored data in the response

trace.note: res.json serializes the full user record

finding.guards_checked: No field filtering or DTO mapping in this file. Whether the stored record contains secrets is unknown because the user model is not in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: none in users.js: no field filtering, DTO mapping, or projection before res.json at users.js:7 and users.js:14. req.user is populated by middleware outside the repo, which is not checked.
verdict.reason: Both trace lines match the claim (users.js:7 is the PUT /me handler's res.json(req.user), users.js:14 is the PUT /me/profile handler's res.json(req.user)), and no filtering exists in this file, but whether the stored user record holds secrets such as password hashes or reset tokens is decided by the user model, which is not in the repo; and the only data returned is the requester's own record (req.user), so even if secrets are present the exposure is to the account owner, not to another role.
